items.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006
items.q: And that’s not to take away from their music but you know, now I know if Brahms was alive today he’d be like what are you guys doing?

ctx.x: That’s an interesting observation. But you know what I can tell you about that. Because at Eastman I mean I had to do a lot of that, I mean obviously playing in operas and playing in the various pieces that we were going to perform for that semester. And basically I think what happens is that you always are in a preparation mode. You’re preparing to play. And so sometimes you can lose the spontaneity. And I don’t think

Mozart or Beethoven wanted that to happen. I think what they wanted to happen was yeah, you know, learn the music. Obviously you have to learn the notes. But you have to get to the music some kind of way. And so what happens is you’re constantly trying not to peak. Because you might only be playing this piece, you know, two or three times. And so if you’re in a rehearsal situation, you know, it’s like well how do you get to the point where it just happens spontaneously, like — for lack of a better definition —…
